prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: [val][adversarial] Feature matrix with long row headers (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 6 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 17px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Capability" · longest unbreakable word 91px · one-line width 411px
  col 2: header "Free" · longest unbreakable word 36px · one-line width 36px
  col 3: header "Team" · longest unbreakable word 44px · one-line width 44px
  col 4: header "Business" · longest unbreakable word 72px · one-line width 72px
  col 5: header "Enterprise" · longest unbreakable word 83px · one-line width 83px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 510px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 509px.
Fixed: content, font, 17px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

These are all candidate designs you produced, rendered in a real browser:
Design r1B: widths [178, 59, 67, 95, 106] · table 506×474px · row heights [39, 92, 92, 92, 92, 66] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r1C: widths [158, 66, 76, 98, 110] · table 509×580px · row heights [39, 118, 92, 118, 118, 92] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r2A: widths [188, 58, 66, 93, 104] · table 510×474px · row heights [39, 92, 92, 92, 92, 66] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r2B: widths [184, 59, 67, 94, 105] · table 510×474px · row heights [39, 92, 92, 92, 92, 66] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r2C: widths [180, 57, 68, 96, 108] · table 510×474px · row heights [39, 92, 92, 92, 92, 66] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r3A: widths [60, 60, 60, 60, 60] · table 301×1633px · row heights [92, 329, 250, 356, 356, 250] · column headers wrapped 4/5 · tallest cell 13 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r3B: widths [60, 60, 60, 60, 60] · table 301×1633px · row heights [92, 329, 250, 356, 356, 250] · column headers wrapped 4/5 · tallest cell 13 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r3C: widths [60, 60, 60, 60, 60] · table 301×1633px · row heights [92, 329, 250, 356, 356, 250] · column headers wrapped 4/5 · tallest cell 13 lines · mid-word splits 0

Decide as a designer:
- "preferred": the best design(s). Name more than one only if they are genuinely equally good.
- "acceptable": other designs a careful designer would still publish.
- "bad": designs with clear visual faults, each with the fault. If none of these is clearly bad, also return ONE deliberately bad but plausible alternative as "contrast" widths and say what is wrong with it.
- "ranges": for each column, the px range within which the preferred design stays equally good (keep other columns' proportions).
- "rationale": 2–4 concrete sentences about this table.
- "principles": observations that seem GENERAL (likely to hold for other tables) vs SPECIFIC to this case.
- "tradeoffs" and "uncertain": what reasonable designers could disagree on.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"preferred":["name"],"acceptable":["name"],"bad":[{"design":"name","why":""}],"contrast":{"widths":[int px],"why":""} or null,"ranges":[[min,max]],"rationale":"","principles":{"general":[""],"specific":[""]},"tradeoffs":"","uncertain":""}

log.raw: {"preferred":["r2A"],"acceptable":["r2B","r1B","r2C","r1C"],"bad":[{"design":"r3A","why":"Equal 60px columns starve the label column: 'Capability' breaks as 'Cap/abilit/y', row labels shatter into 13 one-word lines ('Singl/e', 'work/spac/es'), the table balloons to 1633px tall while a third of the canvas sits empty on the right."},{"design":"r3B","why":"Same fault as r3A — symmetric 60px columns force mid-word fragmentation in every header and label, destroying row unity and making the table unscannable."},{"design":"r3C","why":"Same fault as r3A/r3B — false symmetry of 60px widths trades the only wide column (labels) for width that the tick columns cannot use."}],"contrast":{"widths":[400,27,27,27,28],"why":"Plausible-looking 'give the text room' move, but it pushes the four feature columns below their unbreakable-word widths: 'Business' and 'Enterprise' would break mid-word, tick marks get crammed against the borders, and the label column runs so wide the rows read as prose rather than a matrix."},"ranges":[[172,200],[57,64],[65,72],[93,100],[104,112]],"rationale":"This is a feature matrix, so the reader's task is a diagonal scan: read a capability on the left, then sweep right across four tick columns that must line up in a steady rhythm. The label column therefore deserves the surplus width — r2A's 188px lets 'Single sign-on with any SAML 2.0 identity provider' and 'Data residency in the European Union' break at phrase boundaries rather than mid-phrase, keeping every row at three lines or fewer and the whole table a compact 474px. The four plan columns sit at or just above their minimum unbreakable-word widths (65/93/104 vs 44/72/83 + padding), which is exactly right: headers stay on one line and no cell is padded out with dead space. r1C is publishable but pays a whole extra line per row (580px tall) for a narrower label column, so it is a worse trade, not a different taste.","principles":{"general":["In a matrix with a text label column plus short symbolic columns, spend surplus width on the text column first; symbol columns need only their header word plus padding.","Set short header columns at their longest unbreakable word + padding; extra width there becomes dead space that dilutes the tick rhythm.","Avoid mid-word breaks in headers and row labels — they are the strongest single sign of a mis-proportioned table, worse than an extra line of height.","Equal column widths are only correct when the columns carry comparable content; false symmetry is a fault, not neutrality.","Row height is a cost: an extra line per row across a whole table is a real readability loss unless it buys cleaner phrase breaks."],"specific":["Here the tick columns are 44/72/83px words, so 65–112px each is the entire useful range; anything below 65 breaks 'Team' or 'Business'.","With 509px total and ~411px of one-line label text, the label column can never be one line — the goal is 2–3 clean phrase breaks, which 178–200px achieves."]},"tradeoffs":"A designer could argue r2B or r1B is better balanced: r2A's label column is nearly 4× the Enterprise column, which some would call lopsided, and the four pixels r2A takes from Business/Enterprise buy very little. Conversely one could argue for r1C's more even rhythm at the cost of a taller table.","uncertain":"Whether 188px (r2A) or 184px (r2B) is the sweet spot is within noise — both keep phrase-level breaks, and the choice is essentially arbitrary. It is also debatable whether r1C's 4-line rows are 'acceptable' or a mild fault, since the extra height is uniform and harmless to the scan."}
